title.narrative: NIHR HPSR-CA - Strengthening the health workforce to respond to health impacts of climate crisis in Nepal & Zimbabwe

description.narrative:
The climate crisis is the biggest threat to human health. It is resulting in extreme weather such as heatwaves, droughts, floods and landslides. These events are affecting people emotionally and physically. We are seeing malnutrition, respiratory illnesses, maternal and newborn complications, heat-related deaths, and the spread of diseases such as malaria, and the situation will only worsen. The climate crisis is impacting people’s ability to access health care and health systems’ ability to provide services. We need health systems that can withstand climate shocks and stresses, and the health workforce (HWF) is an important part of that response. If health workers (HWs) do not have the relevant knowledge, skills and support then it will have consequences for health. HWs are well-positioned to talk to people about the climate crisis and to act to protect health and respond to health needs. However, we know that they do not have enough knowledge about the climate crisis and its impact on health. This study aims to change that by developing interventions designed and produced with our chosen communities. Interventions will differ but each will help HWs respond to the health impacts of the climate crisis in their environment. This project will be joint led by Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine and Centre for Sexual Health and HIV AIDS Research Zimbabwe. They will work in partnership with HERD International Nepal from 1st November 2024 to 31st October 2028.
Nepal and Zimbabwe are our country study settings, chosen because they are highly vulnerable to climate crisis. However, they differ in terms of the extreme weather they experience, how their health systems are organised, their geography, their social structures, and their policy frameworks. Together they offer the opportunity to learn different lessons about the climate crisis, its impact on health, and how we can help HWs develop and respond to that challenge - which are lessons useful in other countries facing similar issues. A mix of research tools will help us understand the issues communities face and co-create and implement appropriate interventions. By engaging locally and considering gender and equity we will create interventions that work for everyone. Also, throughout the study we will help those involved learn from their experiences of the research process, whether health systems actors, other stakeholders or researchers in Nepal, Zimbabwe and elsewhere. Together we aim to develop a resilient HWF which is better able to cope with the changing health impacts of the climate crisis, and which can ultimately help save lives.

The project has 4 objectives:
1. To assess preparedness and capacities of health system actors (workers, managers, policymakers and community members including patients and vulnerable groups) to respond to climate crisis related health impacts in Nepal and Zimbabwe. 2. To collaborate with health system actors to co-create context sensitive and gender equitable intervention across both Nepal and Zimbabwe to address climate-related health issues. 3. To monitor and evaluate context-specific pilot intervention packages for equity, feasibility, effectiveness, cost, sustainability and scalability through a mixed-methods approach. 4. Throughout the project duration (2025-2028), facilitate quarterly learning sessions involving health system actors, stakeholders, and researchers in Nepal, Zimbabwe, and globally to share experiences, insights, and adaptations from the research, with the goal of documenting and disseminating at least five key learnings by the end of the project.
